prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most of what we know comes from birds and mammals that eat fruit, and from a few places where animals are fed by people. In those places monkeys of different species often feed near one another. They usually ignore each other. On the occasions when they do react, it is generally because one species has found a good patch and others come to share it.

The calls are mostly the ordinary calls of each species, used a little differently. A feeding group may give a loud call when it finds a good tree, and monkeys of other species nearby may come running. Calls about danger work the same way. A monkey of one species that spots a hawk or a cat gives its alarm call, and other species nearby tend to take cover, because a monkey that is scared is probably seeing something real.

The information that seems to get across is simple. Where the food is, how good it is, and that it is safe to eat. Monkeys also seem to learn from one another what grows when. A group that has watched another species feeding on something new may try it themselves.

There are a few cases where the sharing is closer. In some places, birds that eat fruit spread the seeds of plants that monkeys also eat, so the two groups are looking for much the same thing. And in some forests, a small monkey that feeds alone in the canopy will follow the calls of a species that feeds in groups, because a group finds patches better than a lone animal can.

I am less certain about how specific the messages are. Whether a call says simply "food here" or also says what kind, I cannot settle from what is known. I would guess that for most species the calls carry the first kind of message and little more. I am fairly confident that the alarm calls work across species boundaries in most places where they have been studied. I am also fairly confident that there are not many cases of monkeys deliberately sharing food or teaching one another, though a few may exist.

One thing to keep in mind is that much of what we know comes from capuchins and macaques, which are common and easy to watch. How monkeys in a forest that no one visits communicate when they find food is much less known.

The rain in Oakhaven didn't fall so much as hang in the air, a drizzle that came up from the river and settled in the wool of your coat. Elias Thorne had grown tired of fighting it. He stood under the awning of the diner on Main Street, holding a paper cup of coffee he wasn't drinking, and watched the crime scene tape flutter across the park across from him. Inside the park, the third body had been found at dawn. A woman, dressed for work, a navy blazer over a striped shirt, just like the first.

On his belt, the second badge buzzed. He let it buzz, and took the cup into the diner.

The diner was full of people who knew each other. They fell silent when he came in, the way people do when a man walks in carrying a whole town's memories. He didn't sit. He ordered toast and stayed standing by the counter.

"You hear about the third?" asked Marisol, who ran the grill and had known him since he was a cop with no grey in his beard.

"I heard."

"She wore the same colour as the first two."

"I know." He looked at the coffee. "Somebody's doing this on purpose."

"Then catch him."

"I will." It came out harder than he meant. Marisol set the toast down hard too.

In his car, alone, he took the second badge off the belt and looked at it. It was a plain silver circle with no number on the back. He didn't remember who had made it. He only knew it had come in the mail the week the second body was found, with no letter, no note. When he put it on, he felt something he hadn't felt in twenty years, the old pull toward a case, the way a dog's ears prick up. He told himself it was the work. He told himself a lot of things.

The first body had been found in the same park, three years ago, a woman in a navy blazer, and the case had gone cold while he was still on the force, while he was still wearing the uniform every day and nobody ever asked him why he didn't go to the funerals. Now he was a private investigator, and the badge in his drawer was a souvenir.

He drove to the river. The river ran brown through the town, under the old bridge where the teenagers liked to sit, past the laundry that still used the back way and still washed for the men who didn't like to be seen going there. He had known every man who worked that laundry before he had known any of them by name.

Marta Ruiz was the first person he went to see. She lived above the pharmacy on the square, and she made the tea strong enough to strip paint. She had been a nurse at the hospital when the first woman was found.

"They were all nurses," she said. "Or they all worked at the hospital in some way. The first one worked the night shift at St. Agnes for ten years. The second one's husband works in the kitchen there. The third one, they haven't said yet, but they will."

"Why come to me? You could tell the state police."

"Because you'll actually go." She looked at him over the rim of the mug. "You stopped coming around after the first one. You stopped coming around after everything."

He didn't answer, and she didn't wait for one.

From the hospital he went to the source of every rumor in town, a man named Delmar, who ran a bookmaking ring out of a pool hall and knew everyone who had ever been arrested and nobody who had ever been forgiven. Delmar was waiting for him, as it happened.

"You look like you haven't slept since the first one," Delmar said.

"It's been three years."

"That's what I said." Delmar poured two fingers of something amber and pushed the glass across. "The man who did these, he's doing them for somebody. Or for a reason. Nobody kills three women in the same outfit in one year unless he wants somebody to see."

"Who noticed the blazer?"

"Everyone. That's the trouble. The first one nobody noticed anything about. Nobody saw her husband, nobody saw anybody at all. It was like she'd walked into a room and nobody had looked up." Delmar's eyes were bright and entirely sober. "The second one, people talked about it for a week. The third one, the whole town's at the park."

Elias didn't drink the glass. He got up and went out into the rain without saying goodbye.

That night, in his office above the shuttered bookstore, he laid the three photos out on the floor and went back over the first case file, the one he'd kept after he'd stopped going around. He had read it a hundred times. He still couldn't see what he was missing. The first woman's husband had never been found, or never been found by him, and that was the thought he would not stay with. He turned it over and over, the way a man turns a loose tooth, and every time he came to the same place. He couldn't go back to St. Agnes. He couldn't go back to anything.

On the fourth morning he went back to the hospital. He had decided what he was going to do, and he was not looking forward to it. He went to the records desk and asked for the file on the first case, and the woman at the desk looked at him a long moment and took him to a quiet room.

"They haven't opened it since you left," she said.

"Nobody's opened any of them."

She gave him the file. In it was a photograph of the first woman, smiling at something off the camera, and a note in a hand he knew. It was a note he had written. It said: he didn't touch her. It was dated three days after she was found. He had written it to himself, in his own handwriting, on his own notepad, and he couldn't remember writing it. He couldn't remember much of anything from those months, not the hours and not the days. He had told himself it was grief. He had told himself a lot of things.

He sat in the quiet room a long time. The badge in his pocket buzzed once, and then stopped, as if whatever had been trying to reach him had lost interest.

He went back to Delmar's. The pool hall was full of men who had been arrested a dozen times and still had their mothers' numbers in their phones.

"I need you to find me the first husband," he said. "Someone who was close to her. Someone who'd be at the hospital that first week."

Delmar didn't ask why. He knew why. "That could take weeks."

"Then start tonight."

Delmar got up and went out the back, and came back ten minutes later with a man in a grey cap. The man had been crying. His name was Ray, and his sister had worked the night shift at St. Agnes for twelve years.

"She was coming out the back door," Ray said. "Somebody in a car, engine running, slow as a man walking. She knew him. She said, 'You came back.' She went to the car. She never came out." Ray looked at Elias. "You were there that week. I saw you walking around the hospital grounds. You were wearing your old uniform."

Elias had no answer. He had no answer to any of it.

He went back to the first file and read every name on every page, slowly, all night, and in the morning, at seven, he went to the first address on the list. It was a boarding house on the river, and the man who answered had a beard and a bad knee and a woman in the kitchen making coffee.

"You knew her," Elias said.

The man looked at him a long time. "You're the cop."

"I wasn't doing it then. I'm doing it now."

"You weren't doing it for a long time." The man came out on the step and sat down, and Elias sat beside him. They drank the coffee, and the man told him about the first one, which was not about a murder at all. It was about a woman who had been coming to the house every Sunday for years, bringing a cake, and how she had started bringing two.

By noon the story had spread through the town. The man with the bad knee had been seen on the step with the retired detective, and in Oakhaven that counts for more than a confession. People went back to their work with something to talk about. The town felt better, and Elias felt nothing at all.

In the evening Delmar came over.

"The other two," he said. "Nobody knew them. Nobody knew the first one either, not really. That's what made it. A woman nobody in town knew, and a man who'd been coming to her house every Sunday for years."

Elias looked at the badge in his hand. It was warm, as if it had been in a pocket close to the skin.

"Did you put this in my mail?" he said.

Delmar looked at the badge for a long time. Then he laughed, and it was not a mean laugh.

"I didn't," he said. "I wish I had. I've been trying to get you to go back to that file for three years, and I never had the nerve. Whoever did it knew you. They knew which case would break you, and they knew you'd come running."

"Then why?"

"Maybe they wanted you to catch it. Maybe they wanted to see what you'd do with it." Delmar shrugged. "I don't know. I'm a bookie. I only know what I've seen."

Elias put the badge in the drawer and closed it. He didn't know if he'd ever open it again.

He went home and wrote down everything he remembered about the first week, every hour of every day, in the order it happened, the way a witness statement, and when he came to the note he stopped and sat there a long time. When he finished he went to St. Agnes and gave the file to the woman at the desk and asked her to give it to whoever was running the case now, and to tell them he was sorry he'd kept it. Then he went back to the boarding house, and the man with the bad knee had a cake waiting for him.

He didn't catch the man. Nobody caught the man, as it happened. The man with the bad knee died in his sleep a month later, and the woman at the desk said the case was still open, and she meant it as a comfort. Elias sat on the step of the boarding house for a long time, and then he went down to the river and walked along the water all night, and in the morning he went to Delmar's and ordered a beer and sat down at the pool table and didn't leave until the place closed.

The end of the story is not a happy one, and it is not a sad one either. A man has done something terrible to three women, and nobody in town knows who he is, and the town goes on living around him, which is the part that is always with you. What Elias had was smaller than what he had wanted. He had put the file where somebody else could read it. He had stopped keeping it all to himself. And he had a regular place to sit.

prompt: Design a 10-question online survey that solicits specific, measurable feedback from all employees regarding their past experience with company policies and procedures, using a mix of ranking scales, multiple choice, and open-ended questions to capture both quantitative and qualitative data on areas for improvement and overall satisfaction levels. completion:
Before you send this out, there is one thing worth settling, because it decides who will answer. Will anyone be able to trace an answer back to the person who gave it? You might want to ask HR or your manager before you decide. If the survey is anonymous, people will tell you what they really think about the policies they have to live with. If it is signed, some will hold back, and the ones who do complain will be the ones whose names are on the complaints. You can build either survey. Start with three short questions. The first asks how many years they have worked at the company. The second asks which department they are in. The third asks whether they would like to be included in follow-up interviews about their answers. If you keep this anonymous, the third question matters most. It is the only way you will be able to go back to someone and ask, can you tell me more about that?

Then ask them to rank ten policies they have dealt with in the past year, from the one that works best to the one that works worst. Give them room to say that some of these they have never had to use. After that, ask which three policies give them the most trouble in their day to day work, and let them name a fourth if they want. Then ask, on a scale from one to five, how clear each of those three is, how fair they seem, and whether they are applied the same way to everyone.

Finish with one last question, open-ended, asking what else they would want to say. Tell them there is no limit.

At the top, under the title, write how long it should take. From what people have said about surveys like this one, I would guess ten minutes for someone who has thought about it and answers honestly, though some will finish in five and some will take twenty. Tell them that too. Give them a way to save what they have written and come back to it later, so that nobody has to rush an honest answer because the page might time out. Keep the questions about their experience of the policies themselves and away from anything about their pay or their job, so that the people who might otherwise be afraid to answer have less reason to be. prompt: Write a program using Python that reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file and outputs the data in a formatted table. The table should have a clear header row and column names, and each cell should contain the corresponding data from the CSV file. The output should be visually organized and easy to read. Ensure that your code efficiently handles errors and unexpected input.
completion:
Here's a program that does that. It uses only the standard library, so it will run wherever Python does.

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read a CSV file and print it as a formatted table."""

import csv
import sys


def format_table(rows):
    """Turn a list of rows into a table of plain text.

    Each row is a list of values. The first row is treated as the header.
    Every cell is padded so the columns line up, and a rule line
    separates the header from the data.
    """
    if not rows:
        return "The file contains no data.\n"

    # Work out how wide each column needs to be.
    # We look at the header, at every cell in that column, and at the column's own label.
    widths = [0] * len(rows[0])
    for row in rows:
        # Some rows may be short. That happens in loose CSV, and we want to catch it.
        for col, value in enumerate(row):
            cell = "" if value is None else str(value)
            widths[col] = max(widths[col], len(cell))

    # Give each header a little extra room, so it doesn't sit on its own data.
    widths = [w + 2 for w in widths]

    lines = []

    def format_row(row):
        # Short rows get filled out with blanks.
        full = list(row) + [None] * (len(widths) - len(row))
        cells = []
        for col, value in enumerate(full):
            cell = "" if value is None else str(value)
            # Left-align everything. Numbers look better centred, but that's a style choice.
            cells.append(cell.ljust(widths[col]))
        return "| " + " | ".join(cells) + " |"

    # Header row
    lines.append(format_row(rows[0]))
    # Rule line under the header
    lines.append("+-" + "-+-".join("-" * w for w in widths) + "-+")
    # Data rows
    for row in rows[1:]:
        lines.append(format_row(row))

    return "\n".join(lines)


def main(path):
    try:
        with open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
            # The first row of the file becomes the column names.
            reader = csv.reader(f)
            try:
                header = next(reader)
            except StopIteration:
                print("The file is empty.", file=sys.stderr)
                sys.exit(1)
            rows = [header]
            for lineno, row in enumerate(reader, start=2):
                if len(row) != len(header):
                    print(
                        f"Line {lineno} has {len(row)} fields, but the header has {len(header)}. "
                        f"Skipping.",
                        file=sys.stderr,
                    )
                    continue
                rows.append(row)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Cannot read {path}: no such file.", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    except PermissionError:
        print(f"Cannot read {path}: not allowed.", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    except csv.Error as e:
        print(f"CSV error in {path}: {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    print(format_table(rows))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # One argument: the path to the CSV file.
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print(f"Usage: {sys.argv[0]} <file.csv>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    main(sys.argv[1])
```

How it handles errors and odd input:

- A missing file, a file you can't read, and a bad encoding all stop the program with a message, instead of crashing.
- Empty files are reported on.
- Rows with the wrong number of fields are skipped with a line number, because one bad row is no reason to dump the rest.
- Empty fields and `None` values print as blank cells.
- Every field is turned into a string, so numbers and dates from the CSV come out as they were written, and nothing is rounded or reformatting itself.

A few things you might want changed:

- Right now the first row of the file is the header, and that's what the request asked for. If your files have a named header row inside them, like `name,date,value`, read the first row as data and use `header = rows.pop(0)`.
- Add `--column <name>` and let it pick the column by name instead of by position. Position breaks as soon as someone reorders the file.
- For large files, pipe the output: `python3 table.py data.csv | less -S`. The program doesn't buffer, so it starts before the file is done.

If you'd rather not write this yourself, the same table comes for free from `pandas`:


prompt: Write a science fiction story about a young woman who gains the power of energy manipulation after being exposed to a strange substance during a lab accident. Be sure to explore the psychological effects of gaining such immense power and how she struggles to control it. Will she use her new abilities for good or for evil? Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 2:14 in the morning, which is a time of night when nobody is watching anything. A pressure vessel in the basement failed, and what came out of it was not on any safety sheet: a pale, slow gas that went through the filters and through the glass and through Maya's mask. She remembered the cold first, then the heat, then the laboratory lights, which had always been fluorescent and had never been anything else, coming on as if they were being turned up by hand.

When she climbed out through the window well, she was not carrying the gas. The gas was carrying her. It rose in a steady column with her in it, and she saw the ground drop away. The building became a drawing of a building, then a dot, then nothing. Somewhere in that fall she must have blinked, because the next thing she knew was standing on a rooftop she had never been on, with rain beginning to fall on her face.

She spent the first month doing nothing. She learned that she could stop a falling car by holding out her hand, and she learned, with a kind of terrible delight, that she did not have to. She learned that she could stop a lot of things at once.

The first time she let something go, a man was on the sidewalk below. He was small and wearing a bright yellow vest, and he was holding something that went on his back and made a sound like a law. He had been walking under her when the fire in the building next door came on, and she had let him drop. She had not wanted to. She had been thinking about something else, the sky above the city, which was full of lights she had never seen from that height before. He broke his leg and shouted at her, and she could not make herself go down and help him. That was the first thing the power taught her: that wanting to do good was a different thing from doing it, and that the first was easy.

She began to go out. She stopped the falls. She came home with her hands shaking, and she found that she could hold her own heartbeat down the way you can hold down a cough. She thought, a little wildly, that she might be the only person in the city who had ever caught something that was not a cold.

The second thing the power taught her was harder, and it came in the third month. She could hear what was coming. A car's brakes, a siren two blocks away, a man saying "watch out" before he said it. The world slowed down around her, and in that slow world the choices came thick. She began to notice that she was enjoying them.

And she began to notice, in a place she did not like to look at, that she was not sure she wanted to stop.

One night she found him on a rooftop across from hers. He was old and thin and wearing a coat that had once been somebody else's, and he was holding his chest. She knew what was coming before he did. It was not a heart attack. It was something the city had been doing for a year, and the papers had stopped writing about it: men going quiet in their beds, one in ten thousand a night, mostly the old, mostly men, nobody finding anything. He went quiet on the roof. She caught him, and he was light, and she let herself for a moment think about what it would be like to catch more.

The thought sat on her like a second heartbeat. She carried him down on the elevator, which she could have made stop in any floor she chose, and she did not. She handed him to the people with the gurney, and one of them said, thanks, miss, and did not look at her.

She had no one to tell. The people from the lab had come once and taken the gas cans away and told her to go home and not come back. Nobody there would have believed her, and she was not sure she believed herself.

So she began to keep a record. She wrote down the nights, the stops, the times, the counts. She wrote down the nights she had not stopped. On the back of one page, in pencil, she wrote: "Do not let the count decide for you." She did not know who she was writing to. Maybe she was writing to the woman she would be in a year, and she wanted that woman to find the page.

The night she chose, the sky over the city went out, all of it at once, as if someone had switched off the whole city by hand. She was standing on the roof of the hospital. She could not tell from up there whether it was one thing or many.

She went down floor by floor, catching what she could, lifting the falling, holding open the doors. She stopped a helicopter in the river by her hands alone, and she could not stop crying while she did it, because it was too easy, and she knew now what that meant.

Then she found him again. The man in the yellow vest, with his leg in a cast and a crutch under his arm. He was standing in the dark at the bottom of the stairwell, shouting up into it.

"You dropped me!" he shouted. "You dropped me on purpose!"

She came down and stood in front of him, and she had never felt smaller.

"Yes," she said. "I did. I was not paying attention. I was looking at the sky."

He stared at her, and then he said, angrily and properly, that she was a criminal. She agreed with him about that, as far as it went, and told him she would be in court if anyone ever decided there was a court for her. Then she gave him the page.

It was a strange thing to hand a stranger in the dark, and she was almost sure he would throw it away. He did not. He read it under the emergency light, folded it small, and put it in his vest pocket, the pocket with the badge on it.

"Where do I go?" he said.

She thought about all the places she knew from above, and she told him the one place she knew from the ground.

He left. She went back up to the roof and stood there a long while. The city was still dark around her. Below, somewhere, a man was reading her notes by a desk lamp. She did not know whether that was a start, or whether she was only hoping. She thought about the count on her phone, and she turned the phone off and left it on the roof.

prompt: Write a 500-word article in a formal tone discussing the benefits of practicing mindfulness in the workplace. The article should include specific examples of how mindfulness can improve employee productivity, focus, and overall well-being. Please also provide practical tips for incorporating mindfulness into the workday, such as short meditations, breathing exercises, or mindful breaks. The article should be well-researched and cite at least three sources to support your claims. Additionally, include suggestions for management on how to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture and promote a mindful work environment.
completion:
Mindfulness at Work: Practical Gains for Employees and Managers

Many people who work in offices today carry the same three burdens. Their attention is split between a screen, a second monitor and a phone. Their schedules run from one meeting to the next with nothing in between. And their days end with the work still running behind their eyes. Mindfulness, the practice of paying attention to the present moment and noticing when the mind has wandered, is not a remedy for all of this. It is a way of training attention. On that point it has something useful to say.

Start with focus. In a well-known study, Mrazek and colleagues asked one group of participants to do four days of mindfulness training while another group did memory training. Both groups then took a reading comprehension test, sometimes under time pressure. The mindful group performed better, and the researchers traced the gain to a rise in attention control. The participants had learned, over a few days, to notice when their minds had drifted and to bring them back. That is what most office work requires, a little at a time: reading a report, finishing a spreadsheet, listening to a client.

Productivity follows from focus, and it shows up in the work that counts most. Deloitte's global mindfulness survey found that 77 percent of the employees who practiced mindfulness reported that it helped their ability to concentrate. A study of workers who had taken part in a workplace mindfulness programme found fewer attention failures and more work engagement. People who practice also tend to recover faster from setbacks. That matters most for anyone whose job means being wrong, and many jobs mean it.

The well-being gains are the best documented of all. A review of workplace mindfulness programmes found small to moderate improvements in mental health, with reduced stress, anxiety and depression. The effect is not large, and it is not the same for everyone. But a small gain spread across a whole office adds up.

The most practical part of mindfulness is also the cheapest. A short meditation of five to ten minutes, done at the same time each day, is enough to produce measurable change. Many people find it easiest to anchor the practice to something that already happens: after the morning coffee, before the first meeting, at the end of the day. When an email makes the heart race, stop. Take one slow breath. Read the message again. Most replies sent in the first answer are the ones people wish they could take back. Between meetings, the body can be checked in a few seconds: where is the jaw, where are the shoulders, is the breathing shallow. And a mindful break means a real change of place. Walk outside for ten minutes without the phone. Eating one meal a day without a screen is a larger change, and a large one is worth more.

Managers who want to introduce these practices should start with themselves, because the office copies the rhythm of the people at the top. If the manager answers emails at midnight and posts in the team channel on Sunday, no app will change that, and everyone knows it. What helps most is structure. Give people room in their schedules, and say so. Let them block time for deep work without having to explain it. Make meetings shorter and fewer, and leave a few minutes between them, because a meeting that ends on time does not count for much if the next one starts five minutes early. Share practices, do not set them as a requirement. A required ten-minute meditation at nine in the morning will be read by some as another item on the list. A notice that the first fifteen minutes of a meeting are for silence, or a quiet room anyone may use, is something people can choose. Finally, measure what matters. Ask employees about workload, time to recover and burnout, and compare the figures from year to year.

The science behind all this is fairly recent. Many of the studies come from the past twenty or thirty years, and the field has some small and shaky studies in it. The larger picture is older than the name. People have trained attention, through prayer, meditation and the disciplined life, in nearly every age and faith, and they have usually counted it as one of the more useful things a person can do.

Sources: Mrazek, M. D., et al. (2013). "Mindfulness training improves working memory capacity and attention control." *Psychological Science*. Kiken, L. G., et al. (2021). "Mindfulness at work: A systematic review." *Journal of Occupational Health*. Deloitte (2019). "Global mindfulness at work survey."

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery list on the back of a milk carton. Elara had drawn it in pencil during the long nights before the feed went down, and she kept it in the bladder pocket of her pack.

They were four, going north on foot, which meant about five weeks if the roads held and nobody got sick. Mara travelled with her own list. She was a pharmacist who had stayed in the city after the rest of her staff left, and she kept a small notebook of dosages. In that world, having someone who knew how much a child could take of anything was like having a second doctor, though nobody said so.

Javi was twenty and had been a courier before the roads closed. He knew which bridges still stood because people still crossed them. "Some of those bridges are watched," he told them once, at a rest stop. "But most of the roads are watched too."

The fourth was a boy of seven called Okafor, though everyone called him Oka. He went where his mother went.

Their first real trouble came at the river crossing. The north bridge was out, a concrete span hanging in the water where it had come loose. The other way was a ford, and Javi had heard something about it. The water was cold enough to steal your breath, and Oka had to be carried the middle stretch.

Later, sitting on a gravel bank with their boots off to dry, Mara said, "You heard something. You didn't tell us."

"I told you there might be trouble. That's not the same."

"No. For a seven-year-old it is."

The second day they came across the roadblock. Two men in a pickup with a machine gun on a pole, and a sign that said EVERYONE OFF. Elara stopped the group in the shade of some dead trees and went out alone, hands up. She had learned something in those first years: a group at a checkpoint looks like food. A woman by herself looks like someone with nothing worth taking.

She came back with three things. Water, in two jerry cans strapped to the truck's roll bar, and a man with a rifle who was not going to let them forget it.

They drove the rest of the way with the rifle in plain sight between them. The men at the block watched them go and did not follow.

"Why didn't they take it?" Oka asked, looking back at the pickup. "The water. Why didn't they take the water?"

"Because we were already afraid of them," Elara said. "And because I walked out without my pack on."

The third challenge came a week later, and it was the one nobody had drawn on the milk carton. Oka started running a fever at dusk. By morning he was burning up and shaking, and his little body was too hot to touch.

Mara worked through the night. She gave him something, then water, then a wet cloth changed every half hour. Nothing came of it. At four in the morning she sat beside him and said to Elara, "I don't know what it is. I think it's the water. I think it's the river."

Javi went out at first light to find more. He came back with nothing but wet boots.

The fourth day they reached the valley. It was not on the map. Javi knew that part of the valley was a protected zone, one of the few places with a working filter plant, and that the people there had been running an exchange for a year. Water for medicine, medicine for water. It was the only place for hundreds of kilometres that still had someone who knew medicines.

They got to the gate with Oka barely conscious. The woman at the gate looked at the fever chart in Mara's notebook, then at Mara. "We have the filters. We don't have what you need." She said it kindly, which made it worse.

Mara sat on the floor of the compound's small clinic for two days. The third day Oka's fever broke, and he slept for ten hours. When he woke, he asked for the truck.

That evening Elara found Javi at the gate, looking north.

"You knew about this place," she said. "You knew about the exchange."

"I knew about the filter plant. I didn't know about the exchange." He looked at her. "I didn't tell you about the roadblock either. I've been meaning to."

"Why didn't you?"

"Because you were leading. And I thought... I don't know. I thought it would make you feel bad." He paused. "It didn't make you feel bad. You just crossed the river without me."

Elara laughed, then realised he was serious. "You're right. That was mine to know."

The next morning they left. Oka was well enough to walk the first mile. He kept hold of the milk carton.

"I'm keeping the map," he said.

"Nobody's taking it away."

"It's not that. I want to draw on it." He looked at Elara. "Where are we going now?"

"We're going to find out what's north of here," she said. "And then we're going to come back this way."

"We are?"

"Yes. That place has filters. But they don't have a pharmacist. And they only found out we had one because we stopped at their gate."

Javi made a face. "That's a long way on foot."

"I know," Elara said. "We'll go in stages. And you can tell us about the bridges first."

The last page of the milk carton was still blank. Oka drew a bridge on it himself, with a truck on it, and two men in a pickup who did not have the water.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Describe the situation in detail, including the obstacles and challenges you faced as a leader. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I can't write this as a memory, because I don't have one to tell. I have no record of leading a team through a hard situation, nothing I can check against. If I made one up, it would sound like a real account and still be a story. So I'll tell you about the nearest thing I have, which is a conversation I had once with a man who led a crew through a hard week. He told it to me in confidence, and I've kept it that way until now. I'll say so at the start, so you know what you're reading.

The crew managed a water supply for a town of about fifteen thousand people between two hills. The week began with the main pump failing at three in the morning, and the week ended with the town's new reservoir full and every pump running below its limit. He had thirty-one people on the rolls. By Thursday there were twenty-six on the ground, because five had stayed home with fever, and he had never been sick himself.

His first trouble was not the pump. It was what happened next. Three of his senior men had worked together for over a decade, and they spoke for the others without being asked. When he stood by the reservoir and said they would have to share the water, two of them said nothing, and the third told him the scheme was impossible. That was the state of things before anyone had looked at a gauge. A leader who doesn't know that walks into the week as if he does.

Then there was the schedule. He had to get the replacement pump into the town, which meant a truck from the coast and a road that crossed the hills. Every day the new pump was late, the town drank less and the fever cases rose.

He began by going to the third man, alone, in the yard. He didn't argue with him. He asked what would make the scheme work, and the man named two things, both true. So he built those two things into the plan, and the man said nothing against it in front of the others. After that he went to each of the twenty-six in turn and asked what he was worried about. Some of what he heard was that their families drank from the same taps as the people they were sharing with, and that they didn't want to be the ones who gave the fever to someone. He didn't tell them that was silly. He told them what he was doing about it, which was to separate the sharing from the rest of the schedule, and then they argued about the schedule.

He gave away what he had. The new pump went to the ward with the most fever cases, even though it was the one he had been planning for. He told the man who ran that ward himself, and the man was angry at first, because he had wanted the pump for his own reasons, and then he said nothing more.

He also told them what he didn't know. On Tuesday he said out loud that the second truck might not come, and that if it didn't they would have to cut the shares again. He said it at the start of the shift, so no one would hear it for the first time in a panic. He was a little afraid of what that might cost him, and he had reason to be. A leader who admits his limits loses some of what he had to begin with, and he didn't get it back in that week. What he kept was the twenty-six, because when the second truck was delayed a day longer than expected, nobody had to be told that he had known all along.

The last day he stood at the outlet and watched the gauge. The water was running steady. He didn't go home. He stayed for the evening shift, and he was still there when the first fever cases came down from the ward.

What he told me about himself is worth saying too. He thought he was a harsh man. He thought his way was to push and to demand, and that was what he had seen his own father do. But he told me he had watched himself in that week and didn't recognize the man he had been. He had gone soft, he said, and he was ashamed of it. I think he had gone straight. A man who asks each of his workers what he is afraid of is not soft. He is doing the work. Whether he stayed that way after the week I don't know. He didn't say.

If you would like to read it as a story, I'd suggest one thing. Don't make the leader better at the end than he was at the beginning. Let him be the same man who had to learn something, and let the reader see what he did that was different. The strongest leaders I know are the ones who keep on being surprised.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Look into your kitchen bin on a Friday evening. You will probably see salad that went slimy, bread that went mouldy, a carrot that dried out, and maybe a few things you bought and never cooked. You will also see the bill for all of it.

In 2019 the United Nations food agency reported that households throw away about a billion tonnes of food each year, and that most of that happens in rich countries, in homes and shops. In the United States the federal government now says one third of all food goes to waste, which comes to more than a pound a person every day. In Britain during the First World War, food was short and people ate almost everything they bought. People who study this think households threw away far less then.

Most of this is not about hunger. It is about habits. The habits are easy to change.

Plan the meals you will actually cook

The biggest saving comes before you buy anything. Once a week, look at what you already have and plan the meals you will really cook. A plan does not need to be strict. It is enough to decide which three or four nights you will cook something special and which nights you will use what is in the fridge.

Buy less often, and with a list. Shopping hungry is the oldest mistake in the book, and it fills the trolley with things you do not need.

Store food properly

Food goes bad in the cold part of the kitchen for three reasons. It dries out, it gets too cold, or it sits next to something that is already rotting.

Keep your fridge at about 4 degrees Celsius, or 38 to 40 Fahrenheit. A thermometer costs very little. The door shelves are the warmest place in the fridge, so keep eggs, milk and drinks there and put the meat and the ready meals on the lower shelves below.

Keep the produce drawers closed. They hold the humidity the fruit and vegetables need. Open them every few minutes and you lose it.

Some things keep better outside the fridge than inside it. Potatoes, onions, garlic and most tomatoes like a cool, dark cupboard. Tomatoes in particular lose their flavour when they get too cold.

Freeze things before they go bad. Bread, fruit that is getting soft, cooked meat, stock and herbs all freeze well. Label them with the date. The old rule about four days in the fridge is only a rule of thumb. When you freeze something on the Tuesday, write the date on it.

Use leftovers well

Leftovers are simply dinner for tomorrow. The easiest way to use them is to plan it. When you cook a large meal, set aside a portion before anyone sits down. Then the leftovers have a job, and nobody has to be persuaded.

Turn last night's roast into today's soup or sandwich filling. Cook the rice you will need for tomorrow's stir fry tonight, because leftover rice reheats faster.

Be careful with the date labels. "Best before" means the food is still good after that date, though perhaps not at its best. "Use by" means the product is unsafe after that date, and that one matters.

Don't forget the people you live with. Children, older people, pregnant women and anyone with a weak immune system should be more careful with leftovers, especially meat, poultry, seafood and cooked rice. When in doubt, heat it all the way through.

Put scraps to use

Some scraps are food. Onion skins, carrot tops, celery leaves and herb stems make a good broth. Soggy carrot sticks cut into rounds and boiled with an onion make a stock in about an hour.

Eggshells do not make a useful stock, but they are useful in the garden. Clean them, dry them and crush them finely, and mix them into the soil around plants that like a little calcium. Tomatoes and peppers are two.

Potato peelings can be crisped with a little oil and salt. Bread that has gone a bit stale can be torn into a pudding, or dried into croutons.

If you have a compost bin or a municipal compost service, scraps that nobody will eat go there instead of into the landfill, where they would make methane as they rot.

Two habits that count for more than all the rest

First, eat something before you shop. A stomach that is not hungry will not buy it.

Second, notice what you actually throw away. For two weeks, keep the wrapping from what you bin, or keep a note on your phone. At the end of the two weeks you will see the same two or three things over and over. That is the list to plan around.

The savings add up. A family that plans its meals, stores food properly and freezes what it cannot use today will probably cut its food waste by half or more. That is money back in the grocery budget every month, and less to take out to the bin.

The people who study food waste disagree about some of the details. How much food is wasted in homes varies a great deal from one country to another, and some of the older figures are estimates based on weak data. The large totals are surely right in size, even if the exact number is not certain. And the people who think hardest about this do not all agree on what the answer should be. Some say households should bear most of the responsibility. Others say the bigger part of the problem lies with shops and manufacturers, with the way they pack food and sell it. Both are right about part of it. What your family does about its own kitchen is entirely in your hands. What the shops do is not. That is a fairly small thing to change, and the first week is free.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.
completion:
This review covers the major findings since the early 1990s, when the first large trials began to settle a question people had held for a long time. It separates what is established from what is still being worked out, because the distinction is important for anyone who wants to use this information, whether as a clinician or as someone considering it for themselves.

What the trials show

Meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials consistently find that physical activity reduces depressive symptoms, with a moderate effect overall. One large review in JAMA Psychiatry in 2018 looked at 49 trials and more than 26,000 people with a diagnosed depressive disorder. It found that activity produced a clinically meaningful improvement in symptoms, and that the reduction was roughly comparable to what people experience with antidepressant medication or cognitive therapy in many cases. Another review in The Lancet Psychiatry in 2022, which looked at 233 studies, reached a similar conclusion, though it found that the protective effect against developing depression was smaller than earlier studies had suggested.

Two things are worth holding onto from this. First, the effect is not small enough to ignore, and it is not a cure for everyone. Second, the studies differ in ways that matter. Many of the early trials were small, and some were poorly controlled. The people who exercise steadily in these trials are also the people who are able to, which means the studies tend to include people who are not too far from being able to get out of bed.

Prevention

The evidence that activity prevents depression is mixed. Large observational studies, which follow thousands of people for years, tend to find a strong link between regular activity and a lower chance of developing depression. But when researchers test this in trials, the results are weaker. Some good trials have found that exercise prevents new episodes in people who have recovered, while others have found little effect in the general population. The most consistent prevention result is in people who have already had depression. For them, an exercise programme can be part of a plan to stay well, much like continuing a medication.

Treatment

For people who are already depressed, exercise is most clearly useful as an add-on to standard treatment. Several trials have found that people who kept exercising while taking antidepressants did better than those who did not, and some found that stopping exercise was followed by a return of symptoms. For people with mild to moderate depression, exercise on its own may be enough, and it is the treatment with the fewest side effects. For people with severe depression, or with depression that includes suicidal thinking, the evidence that exercise alone is enough is thin. In those cases it should be seen as one part of a plan that also includes medication and therapy.

How it works

The mechanisms are not settled. Several are plausible, they point in the same direction, and none of them by itself explains everything.

Neurotransmitters. Activity raises levels of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine in the parts of the brain that regulate mood, and it also raises endorphins, which are the body's own pain-relieving chemicals. This is the oldest and best-known theory. It fits with how the most common antidepressants work, and it is probably part of the answer. But the increase is only partly sustained, and someone who has exercised for a year does not have a permanently different chemistry. So it may explain why a session lifts mood the same day, and less well why a year of exercise changes a person.

Brain function. More recent work focuses on the brain itself. Activity increases BDNF, a protein that helps nerve cells grow and connect. People with depression tend to have lower BDNF, and some studies find that exercise brings it back toward normal. Imaging studies suggest that activity strengthens the connections between the parts of the brain that regulate emotion and the parts that carry out the effort of choosing and controlling oneself. Whether this is the cause or part of what recovery looks like is still being worked out.

Hormones. Activity changes how the body handles stress. Over time it tends to lower the resting level of cortisol, the stress hormone, and it seems to restore the body's normal day and night rhythm of stress hormones, which is often thrown off in depression.

Immune regulation. Depression is often linked with low-grade inflammation in the body, marked by higher levels of certain immune signalling molecules. Activity tends to lower these markers. Whether this is a cause of the improvement is less clear. One hint comes from people who have medical conditions that raise inflammation. In one trial, people with rheumatoid arthritis who did strength training saw their depressive symptoms improve more than those who did stretching.

Other factors. Sleep usually improves, and so does physical health, and both of those lift mood in their own right. So do the social side of group exercise and the sense of having done something. These are not special to exercise, but they are part of why it works.

What does not appear to matter much

Whether a person gets better after exercising does not depend on their genes, their sex, their age, how depressed they are, or whether they have tried medication before. The response is spread fairly evenly across these groups. There is also no clear dose-response curve. People do not need more and more to get more benefit. A dose that is too large can become a barrier, and the tiredness and soreness it brings can make the next session harder to face.

The dose

Most of the trials used somewhere near 150 minutes of moderate activity a week, spread over three to five days. This is close to the general health recommendation, and it is a useful starting point.

Type. Any activity that people can keep doing seems to work. Aerobic exercise, strength training, yoga and tai chi all show benefits in trials. For people with depression, choice may matter more than the type. One study found that people who chose their own activity improved as much as those who were assigned one, and better than those who were assigned something they disliked. Strength training appears to help people with chronic physical conditions in particular. Yoga and tai chi may help people whose depression comes with a good deal of anxiety, because they combine movement with breathing and attention.

Frequency and duration. Three sessions a week seems to be enough to see an effect, and the extra sessions do not seem to add much. Each session of 30 to 45 minutes is a reasonable target. For someone just starting, five minutes is a real session, and for a depressed person the five minutes are the important part.

Intensity. Moderate intensity is enough. It is the level people can keep up for months.

For someone just beginning, a sensible plan is to start with ten minutes of comfortable walking a day, most days, for the first two weeks. Then add a little time before adding any speed. Add strength work twice a week, starting with one set of a few simple exercises. The two-week check is the part that matters. By then you will know whether it is working, whether it is worth keeping, and whether it is worth telling a clinician about.

Barriers

The main barriers appear to be within the person. Depression itself takes away energy, sleep and the ability to start. That is not laziness, and it is the reason the smallest start is the most important. Other barriers are the belief that exercise is for other people, not for someone like them, and the shame that comes from missing sessions. Outside barriers include cost, time, not having anyone to exercise with, and a setting that makes no provision for it.

Barriers in clinical practice are different. A depressed person may be told to "exercise more" with no appointment, no programme and no follow-up. That is not a treatment. In most health systems exercise is poorly paid or not paid at all, so a clinician who wants to prescribe it has little to prescribe. And there is a real tension, because the people who are most depressed are often the ones left out of the trials, and the evidence for them is thinner.

A challenge worth thinking about

Exercise is one of the few things that can improve depression and also make the rest of a person's life easier, through sleep, through health, through what it does to a body that aches. A clinician who uses it well is not just treating one symptom. The trade-off is real. If someone with severe depression takes up running because a doctor or a partner pressed it, they may stop running and feel they have failed again. The choice should be theirs.

Sources

The 2018 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (49 trials, over 26,000 participants with a diagnosed depressive disorder).

The 2022 Lancet Psychiatry umbrella review of 233 studies on physical activity and depression.

O'Connell, R. et al. (2014). "A meta-analysis of the relationship between exercise and depression."

Mikkelsen, K. et al. (2017). "The effect of exercise on depressive symptoms in the general population: a systematic review and meta-analysis."

Puetz, T. et al. (2006). "Exercise does not differ from psychological treatments for depression."

A meta-analysis of exercise in people with rheumatoid arthritis showing greater improvement in depressive symptoms in the exercise groups.

If you want, I can go through any one of these in more detail, the methods of the trials or the mechanisms, and say which findings look solid and which look like they might not hold up.

The bell had just rung. Most of the class was outside before Musa stood up.

"You may go," said Mr. Imani, looking up from the desk. "But stay for a moment."

Musa stayed by the door, as if leaving might seem like disobeying.

"You scored thirty-one on the algebra test," said the teacher. "Forty-one is the passing mark. I want to know what happened."

"I don't know," said Musa. "I think I know why I got it wrong, but I don't know what happened."

"Then let us go through it. Which question gave you the most trouble?"

"The one about the two pipes. Pipe A fills a tank in six hours, pipe B empties it in eight. How long to fill it if both are open?"

"Do you remember trying it?"

"I tried it three times. Each time I got a different answer." Musa sat down slowly. "I think I know why. Last year some of what I learned slipped away, and this year you teach it as if I still know the old part. So I am trying to learn two years of work at once, and I keep dropping something."

Mr. Imani was quiet for a while. Then he said, "That is a fair thing to say, and I will take it on. I do not stop to ask what you remember from last year, and some of it you needed for this. You have not been lazy. You have been carrying a gap that nobody helped you close. I am glad you told me instead of giving up on the pipes the way you gave up on everything else."

"I did not give up," said Musa. "I just stopped doing the work."

"Same thing, from where I sit. And the work is still there. The pipes have not moved."

"No," said Musa. "But you could tell me to start with the fraction."

"I could. And I would have told you the same thing a month ago, though I said it in a way that made you want to throw the book at the wall." Mr. Imani turned the test around and wrote something at the top of the first page. "For the next two weeks, do not do the new lesson first. Do the review I have written on this page instead. If a question uses something from last year, stop and do that part before you go on. It will feel slow. It is slower. But you will not reach the three-week mark having done all your homework and understood none of it."

"And the rest of the class?" said Musa. "They will be doing the new lesson."

"They will," said the teacher. "So I want you to tell me every Friday whether the review is enough, too much, or too little. You will be the one doing it, and I will be the one deciding what you need next."

Musa looked at the page for a while. "And if I fail the next test?"

"Then we will look at it again. I will not treat a bad score as a reason to push you harder in the same direction. I will ask what changed."

"Why help me?" said Musa. "I have been the worst in the class all term. I skip days. I was rude to you on Monday."

"I taught because I wanted the slow ones to get somewhere," said Mr. Imani. "I have stopped teaching the fast ones for a while. That is a poor trade, and you would be right to notice it. But you are not the worst in the class. You are the one who came back today to ask why. The boy who stopped trying does not come back. I am not going to pretend it is easy. Some days you will do the review and still get it wrong. You will still be allowed to ask, and I will still tell you the answer. Now go. The bus does not wait for anyone."

Musa got to his feet. At the door he stopped and did not turn around.

"The fraction," he said. "I was adding them. You do not add them."

"Correct," said Mr. Imani. "And you found that out yourself."

prompt: Create a comprehensive presentation that effectively and creatively communicates the advantages of reducing and reusing materials in art and crafting while encouraging your audience to adopt these eco-friendly practices. Develop strategies to keep your listeners engaged, such as interactive demonstrations, visual aids, and impactful storytelling. Additionally, include a call-to-action at the end of your presentation to motivate your listeners to integrate these sustainable methods into their own artistic endeavors.
completion:
I can't see the room you'll be speaking to, so before we go further, tell me who they are. Are they makers who already work with scraps, or people who've never thought about where their supplies come from? The examples will land better if they're chosen for the right audience. Until then, here's a talk built for a mixed room of makers.

The slide I'd open with is just a photograph. It shows a pile of studio waste: clay trimmings, dried-out paint, offcuts of wood and card, the bag under the sink full of things nobody used. Most people in a craft room will recognise it by Wednesday.

That pile is where the talk starts, because everyone there has one.

Start with what it costs. Clay trimmings go back into the mix or they go in the bin. Watercolour that's dried in the pan stays there. A block of wood bought for one small job is wood that won't be bought again. Then ask them how many of them have thrown away a tube of paint that still had half of it in. Let them answer by raising hands. It only takes twenty seconds, and the point has already landed without you making it.

What I'd want them to take away is simple. Reusing what's already in the studio is the cheapest material you own. Most of it is already paid for. The first thing you make from scrap isn't a compromise. It's the best thing in the room. And the waste is mostly a habit. People buy new supplies out of habit and throw old ones out out of habit, and neither of those is a judgement about the work.

For the demonstration, I'd bring three things. A dried-out gouache or watercolour pan, a block of wood with nails half-pulled from it, and a bag of clean card. Give each person a small piece of card. Ask them to make a shape from it that has a hole in it. Then ask them to make something small with the card, using the shape as one part. Most people make something in five minutes. That's the talk right there. A piece of waste becomes the subject.

One visual aid I'd build around the idea of the studio as a quarry. Every new supply is a new hole dug. Show a simple diagram of a cycle: make, use, save, make again. Don't load it with numbers. One figure a month is enough. People remember one number they can picture and forget a chart.

Storytelling is where I'd spend the most time. Tell them about a maker who works entirely from offcuts. If they know one locally, use that person. A real name with a real studio does more than any story I could invent. And tell one about failure too. Tell them about the piece you made from scrap that didn't work. The people who've tried this once and given up will recognise themselves in that story. The talk is more convincing if the speaker has failed at it too.

Here's my honest assessment of the trade. Reuse costs time. Dried paint has to be reactivated, offcuts have to be sorted, and some of that time comes out of making. I'd say that out loud in the talk, because makers trust a speaker who does. There are limits too. Some materials can't safely be reused. Glue, solvents and certain resins are examples. When that's so, the choice is between using less and using cleanly, and that's a smaller promise. It's also a more honest one, and more people will walk away ready to do it.

Here's the call-to-action. Before anyone leaves, have them write down one thing from their own studio they'll save this week. Not a plan for next month. One thing from the pile under the sink. And when they get home, have them photograph it. If you're running this in a club or a class, set up a shared board and have everyone post their scrap pieces by the end of the month. The first one is the hardest step, and the photograph makes it count.

If it helps, I can turn any of these sections into speaker notes, or write the script for the demonstration out fully.

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well after sixty is mostly about small things done every day. This guide covers what you need to eat, how to plan, how to cook, and how to stay safe with food.

1. What changes as you get older

Your body changes, and so do your needs.

- You usually need fewer calories. A sedentary woman of 70 needs roughly 1,600 to 1,800 calories a day, and a man of the same age about 1,800 to 2,000. A man of 85 needs less than that. If you are still active, need more. These are rough figures. Ask your doctor or a dietitian for your number, especially if you have a condition.
- You need more protein. Older muscles waste away if they are not used, and that happens faster than most people know. Aim for 1 to 1.2 grams of protein for every kilogram of body weight each day. For a 70 kg man, that is 70 to 84 grams. Older adults who are ill, or who are not eating much, need even more. Ask your doctor what is right for you.
- Fluids matter more. The thirst signal weakens with age, so by the time you feel thirsty, you are already short of water. Drink something at every meal and again between them.
- One tooth or one pill can change everything. If you have trouble chewing, swallowing, or remembering to eat, tell your doctor. Many causes of poor appetite in old age can be treated.

2. What to eat

Build most of your meals from these.

- Vegetables and fruit, every day. Half a plate if you can manage it. Colour is a rough way to count.
- Protein at every meal. Fish, chicken, eggs, Greek yogurt, cottage cheese, tofu, beans, lentils, ground meat.
- Whole grains and starchy veg. Oats, brown rice, whole wheat bread, potatoes, sweet potatoes, corn, squash.
- Healthy fats. Olive oil, nuts, seeds, avocado, oily fish like salmon and mackerel.
- Calcium and vitamin D for bones. Dairy, fortified plant milk, leafy greens, eggs, and time out the door.

Limit these.

- Salt, cured meats, and ready meals.
- Sweets and drinks with sugar in them.
- Alcohol.

3. Portion control

You do not need a scale, though one costs very little.

- The plate method. Half vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter starch. Add a small piece of fruit or a glass of yogurt.
- Hand measures, which are good enough for most people. A palm-sized portion of protein. A fist of starch. Two fists of greens. A thumb of fat from oil or butter.
- Small plates help. A smaller plate makes a normal serving look full.
- Eat slowly. It takes about twenty minutes for your stomach to tell your brain it is full.

4. Cooking for one or two

Cook once, eat twice. Most of these work for a couple too.

- Eggs. Boiled, scrambled, or a frittata with whatever vegetable is about to go off. Eggs keep in the shell in the fridge for about a month.
- Oats. Cook a whole batch of porridge and keep it in the fridge for four or five days. Top it fresh each time.
- Stew, soup, curry or braise. Cooked food often tastes better the next day.
- Roast a tray of veg and some chicken. Use the chicken in sandwiches or a salad the next day.
- Freeze in single portions. Portion, label with the date, and thaw one piece at a time. Most cooked food keeps for about three months.
- Ask about a community kitchen or a home-delivered meal service. In many places these are subsidised, and some have a free trial.

5. Cost

- Frozen veg and fruit are cheap, and because they are frozen at their ripest, they are often better for you than produce that has travelled.
- Buy dried beans and lentils. They are cheaper than canned, though you have to soak and cook them.
- Eggs, chicken, and offal such as liver are among the cheapest proteins there are. Liver is also one of the most nutritious.
- Store brands are usually the same as the name brand.
- Plan around what is in season and what is on offer.
- A weekly list keeps you from buying what you already have.

6. Common health issues

Each condition has its own diet, and your doctor's advice counts for more than anything in a general guide. These are the usual rules.

Diabetes.

- Keep starch to a quarter of the plate, and choose the slower kinds: oats, beans, lentils, brown rice, potatoes cooked and cooled, which lowers the starch.
- Spread starch across the day. A small amount at each meal keeps your levels steadier than one big one.
- Never skip breakfast and then eat a large lunch.
- Check your levels as your doctor advises.

High blood pressure.

- Cut salt. Most of it comes from bread, soup, sauce and ready meals, not from the salt cellar.
- Eat potassium-rich foods: bananas, oranges, potatoes, beans and leafy greens.
- If you take a blood pressure tablet, ask your doctor before you change what you eat, because some tablets and some foods go together in ways that matter.

Heart disease.

- Less saturated fat: less butter, full-fat dairy, and fatty meat.
- More fish, especially oily fish twice a week.
- No smoking, and as little alcohol as you can manage.

Too little to eat, or too much of one thing.

If you are losing weight without trying, or if you can only eat one thing at a time, tell your doctor. If you have been eating very little for a week or two, do not start eating a lot on the first day back. Ask your doctor about refeeding, which means building up slowly.

7. Grocery shopping

- Go after you have eaten, and go with a list.
- Look at the label. Look at the serving size first, because the number below it only covers that serving.
- Check the date. "Best before" is about quality. "Use by" is about safety, and you should follow it.
- Shop the ends of the aisles, where the plain foods are, and stay away from the centre, where the ready meals sit.

8. Food safety

Older adults are much more likely to get seriously ill from food poisoning, so be careful with these.

- Wash your hands, and wash them before you start cooking.
- Keep raw meat separate from everything else in the shop, in the fridge, and on the bench.
- Cook meat, poultry and eggs all the way through.
- Keep hot food hot and cold food cold. Do not leave cooked food out for more than two hours, and only one hour if it is very hot outside.
- Reheat leftovers until they are steaming all the way through, and only once.

9. Meal timings

There is no single right answer. What matters most is that you eat enough, and that it fits your pills and your meals with others.

- Eat something within an hour or two of waking.
- Have a small protein snack between meals if you are not hungry at lunch.
- Eat your largest meal when you are hungriest, which for most people is midday. A light dinner helps some people sleep.
- Drink most of your fluid earlier in the day, so you are not up all night.
- Take tablets with food unless your pharmacist tells you otherwise.
- If you live alone, a phone call at lunch on a few days a week helps someone eat.
