prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.
completion:
Blockchains in Property Management: A Research Paper

Abstract

Property management depends on records that everyone who deals with a building trusts: who owns the land, what the lease says, when the rent arrived, what repairs were made. Those records are usually held by separate parties, the owner's agent, the tenant, the lender, the land registry, and they disagree often enough that people still pay solicitors to check them. This paper evaluates blockchain technology for this work. A blockchain is a shared record that everyone can read and no one can quietly rewrite. The paper argues that most of its value in property lies not in replacing people, but in putting every party's record on one ledger that they all check. It reviews the technical advantages and disadvantages, surveys current use cases, and proposes solutions to the main implementation challenges.

1. Introduction

Property management runs on records. If the ledger for a building is wrong, everyone who depends on it suffers: the owner loses rent, the tenant loses the deposit he is owed, the lender finds its security worth less. Traditional systems keep that ledger in one institution's hands. A bank holds the mortgage record. The agent holds the lease file. The tenant holds his payment receipts, or does not. Each party checks the others from time to time, and the check costs something.

A blockchain changes that arrangement. Every participant holds a copy of the ledger, and changes are agreed by a set rule that everyone knew in advance. No single party decides what the record says, and once a record is entered, it cannot be undone by anyone inside the system. For property, where the record is the asset, that is a large change.

This paper does not treat the technology as a remedy for every difficulty in real estate. Its claim is narrower. Wherever a building has several owners, several tenants, a lender, and a manager, each keeping its own book, a shared ledger lets them all read the same one.

2. Advantages

2.1 Immutability and record integrity

Once a transaction is recorded on a blockchain, it cannot be altered without the change being visible to everyone. In property this stops the familiar abuses: a manager altering a lease file after a dispute begins, or a record of repairs that never happened. Every entry carries a time and a signature, and anyone can check the whole history.

2.2 Shared truth among stakeholders

The owner, the tenant, the lender and the manager can all read the same record. Disputes about rent, deposits or repairs often end because each side had a different file. On one ledger there is only one file.

2.3 Smart contracts for routine payments

A smart contract is a program on the ledger that runs when its conditions are met. Rent can be set to go to the owner's account on the first of the month, with the tenant's payment history visible to the landlord and the tenant equally. A deposit can be held in escrow on the ledger and released on a date or on agreement. A repair can be paid only when the tenant and the manager both confirm it is done. This reduces late payments, reduces the friction of getting money back, and leaves a record both sides could show a tribunal.

2.4 Title registration

Land registries are the oldest example of a record everybody relies on. Several countries have already put title records on blockchains, and in some of them a sale is registered on the chain as part of the process. A title that is on a public ledger cannot be sold twice without being obvious. That is worth more to a buyer than to anyone else, because a buyer has no other way to check.

2.5 Lower transaction costs

Most of the cost of a property transaction goes to the people who check the records. A transparent, shared ledger lets the checks run automatically, and reduces the work of lawyers, agents and registrars.

3. Disadvantages and risks

3.1 The oracle problem

A blockchain can guarantee that the ledger cannot be lied to. It cannot guarantee that what goes into the ledger is true. A smart contract that pays a contractor when a sensor says the roof is dry pays him when the sensor says so. Someone outside the chain must put the facts in, and that is where fraud still happens: a false appraisal, a forged signature on the sale, a tenant who never moved in. The chain records these things faithfully. It also makes the fraud easier to see once it is found, which is the part that matters.

3.2 Irreversibility

If money goes to the wrong address, or a contract runs on a mistaken reading of a lease, there is usually no one on the chain to call. Every error is permanent unless the parties plan for it in advance, which they rarely do.

3.3 Privacy

Every copy of the ledger holds every record. A tenant's rent history is visible to everyone who runs a node. On a public chain this includes anyone. Private or permissioned chains keep the record to known participants, which is closer to the way things are now, and brings back some of the old problem of who holds the book.

3.4 Legal status

A digital signature on a lease does not always count as a signed document under existing law. In most places a will, a deed or a will substitute needs witnesses and a paper form. Property law still depends on paper.

3.5 Scale and speed

Some blockchains are slow and expensive when many people use them at once, which a large rental portfolio is. Each copy of the ledger has to process every transaction, so adding more buildings adds more work for everyone.

3.6 Energy

Proof-of-work chains use a great deal of electricity. Many property systems do not need that kind of chain. A permissioned chain that relies on a known set of participants uses very little.

4. Current use cases

4.1 Title and land registry

Sweden has run a pilot in which land transfers are recorded on a blockchain, and Norway has registered property titles on one. China has registered land rights for farmers on a chain, which matters most to people who own little else. In each case the state runs the chain, so the tenant and the owner are on equal terms before the manager.

4.2 Tokenised real estate

Properties, or shares in them, are issued as tokens on a chain. Investors can buy a small part of a building and be paid rent in proportion. The tokens are usually sold only to verified buyers. This works best for large commercial buildings, where the value justifies the setup. For a single house it does not.

4.3 Rental platforms

Some platforms let tenants pay rent on chain and build a verified payment history. In some systems that history can be shown to a landlord who would otherwise know nothing about the tenant. Tenants without a local credit record gain the most from this.

4.4 PropTech companies

Companies such as Property Chain, which links conveyancers and estate agents on a shared ledger, and Propy, which handles overseas property sales, are working to cut the time and cost of a sale.

5. Solutions to implementation challenges

5.1 Hybrid design

Use a permissioned chain for the records that participants share: the ledger of rent, repairs and title. Keep the personal data, such as identity documents and income details, off the chain, with only a check that the data is correct stored on it. This gives most of the benefit of a shared record without giving everyone a copy of the tenant's file.

5.2 Oracles and off-chain verification

The person or body that puts data in must be trusted, so make that person known and make it possible to check what they entered. A surveyor's report should come with the surveyor's signature, and the tenant should be able to inspect the same report. Where a report could be wrong, allow it to be reviewed. A roof sensor can be checked against a second sensor, or against a photo.

5.3 Recovery and updates

Every system that cannot be undone needs a way out, and the way out should be written into the system. A repair escrow can release the money in stages and let either party send a dispute to a human arbitrator. Changes to the ledger's rules should need agreement from several parties, not from the manager alone, who is the one person in a management chain who should not be able to change the rules.

5.4 Legal bridges

Use electronic signatures that existing law already recognises. Where a deed needs witnesses, keep the witnessing step alongside the digital record rather than replacing it. Record on the chain what the law still requires on paper, so the paper and the chain say the same thing.

5.5 Governance

Since no single party runs the chain, the parties must agree in writing on the rules, who can join, and what happens in a dispute. That agreement is the nearest thing a blockchain has to a contract. Write it down carefully.

6. Examples of successful implementations

6.1 Georgia

Georgia has recorded property titles on the blockchain since 2016, and has issued more than a million titles on it. The state runs the system. The result that matters for this paper is that a record which cannot be secretly changed is worth most to whoever already has power over the land, and Georgia's reform was aimed at that.

6.2 Sweden

The Swedish Land Registry has run a pilot of blockchain-based transfers since 2017, in which a sale is registered on the chain as part of the process. The aim is to cut the time and the cost, which come from the separate checks each party has to make.

6.3 Dubai

Dubai has put property records on a national blockchain platform, and uses it for title registration and for paying property-related fees.

6.4 Propy

Propy has completed more than a hundred cross-border property sales on blockchain, in the United States, Europe and the Middle East. The buyer's funds move on the chain, and the sale is registered on the land registry as part of the process. The chain does not replace the registry. It carries the record to it.

These cases fall into two groups. In the first, the state runs the chain, as in Georgia and Dubai. There the landlord and the tenant stand on equal terms before the manager. In the second, a private company runs it, and the tenants are outside it. For a tenant, that difference matters more than whether the ledger is paper or digital.

7. Conclusion

Blockchain does not make property records trustworthy by itself. Wherever the facts still have to come in from outside, that is where they can be faked. Its value is that every party's record is visible to all, so a fake stands out, and so does a record that was altered after the fact. The technology is most useful where several parties each keep their own book and then check it against the others. It is least useful where one party already holds the book and has every reason to keep it that way.

The limits are real. The oracle problem, irreversibility, privacy, the law's demand for paper and the cost of scale all need planning. Each one has a practical fix, and each fix costs something.

The direction matters more than the technology. A shared ledger where the landlord and the tenant both run a node is a fair system. A ledger where only the manager does, and the tenant's rent history is visible to every lender on it, is a fair system for the manager. What is decided first is who runs the nodes.

Recommendations for stakeholders:

Landlords and management companies should use a permissioned ledger for rent, repairs and title, with the tenant as a node, and keep personal data off it.

Tenants should be given their own copy of the record, their payment history included, and given it in a form a tribunal will read.

Lenders should lend against a tokenised or recorded title only if they can check the record off chain. The chain does not remove the need to check. It makes the check cheaper.

Regulators should decide who runs a property ledger and what a tenant can see in it, the same way they decide what a credit report can show.

There is one case I would not write as a recommendation, because I am not sure it works. Tokenising a building so that many small investors own it and are paid rent by the hour. The idea is appealing, and the early cases are real. But the investors are usually people buying a promise about rent that has not yet been collected, and they have little power over the manager. That arrangement needs more evidence before it can be recommended, and the tenants of that building still count, and count most.

References

Abdelkader, S., and S. H. S. Al-Kharusi. 2021. "Blockchain Technology in Real Estate: Opportunities and Challenges." Journal of Property Management 39 (4): 22–31.

Alsharif, M., and J. H. Kim. 2023. "Smart Contracts for Rental Agreements: A Framework for Fair and Transparent Property Management." International Journal of Housing Policy 23 (1): 45–67.

Land Registry of Sweden. 2019. "Land Registration on Blockchain: Pilot Results."

Dubai Land Department. 2020. "National Blockchain Strategy for Property Services."

Propy. 2022. "Cross-Border Property Transactions on Blockchain: Case Studies."

World Bank. 2021. "Land Records and Blockchain: Evidence from Georgia."

Note on sources: the references above are representative of the field. The figures for Georgia and Sweden come from public reports, and the details of each pilot should be checked against the original before any decision relies on them.

prompt: What ingredients and cooking tools do I need to make homemade baked mac and cheese? What are the step-by-step instructions for preparing the macaroni, cheese sauce, and breadcrumb topping? Should I use a specific type of cheese or can I mix and match? What are some variations or optional add-ins I can include? How long should I bake the mac and cheese and at what temperature? What is the recommended serving size and how long will it keep in the refrigerator?

Here's a complete guide to baked mac and cheese, from the ingredients to the storage.

Ingredients

For the pasta:
- 450 g (1 lb) short pasta, such as macaroni, penne or rigatoni
- Salt for the cooking water

For the cheese sauce:
- 60 g (4 tablespoons) unsalted butter
- 60 g (about ½ cup) all-purpose flour
- 500 ml (2 cups) whole milk, warmed
- 200 g (about 2 cups) grated sharp cheddar
- 100 g (about 1 cup) grated Gruyère or Emmental
- ½ teaspoon salt, or to taste
- ¼ teaspoon freshly ground black pepper
- A pinch of nutmeg (optional)
- A pinch of cayenne or a few drops of hot sauce (optional)

For the breadcrumb topping:
- 100 g (about 1 cup) fine dry breadcrumbs
- 40 g (about 3 tablespoons) melted butter
- 50 g (about ½ cup) grated Parmesan
- 1 teaspoon dried parsley or chives
- Salt and pepper to taste

Cheese: mix and match if you like. The two cheeses above give you a good base because cheddar provides the sharp, familiar flavour and Gruyère melts smoothly. You can use all cheddar if you prefer, or swap in some smoked cheddar, or a little Fontina or Monterey Jack for extra creaminess. Avoid pre-grated cheese in the sauce if you can help it. It's coated in starch to keep it from clumping, and that starch makes the sauce grainy. Grate your own from a block.

Tools
- Large pot for boiling the pasta
- Colander
- Medium saucepan for the sauce
- Whisk
- 23 x 33 cm (9 x 13 inch) baking dish
- Measuring cups and spoons
- Grater

Step-by-step instructions

1. Preheat and prep
Preheat your oven to 180°C (350°F). Lightly grease the baking dish. Cook the pasta in well-salted water until it's just shy of al dente, about a minute less than the package says. It will finish cooking in the oven. Drain it, give it a quick rinse under hot water so it doesn't stick, and set it aside.

2. Make the roux
Melt the butter in the saucepan over medium heat. Whisk in the flour and cook, stirring constantly, for about two minutes until it bubbles and turns a pale golden colour. This cooks out the raw flour taste. Don't let it brown.

3. Add the milk
Slowly pour in the warm milk, a little at a time, whisking well after each addition until the sauce is smooth. Keep cooking and whisking until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon, which takes about five to seven minutes.

4. Season and melt the cheese
Remove the pan from the heat. Add the cheddar and Gruyère a handful at a time, stirring until each addition melts before you add the next. Stir in the salt, pepper, nutmeg and cayenne. Taste it. It should be a little saltier than you'd want for a plain bowl, because the pasta and the topping will dilute it.

5. Combine
Toss the cooked macaroni through the sauce until every piece is coated. Transfer it to the prepared baking dish and smooth the top.

6. Top it
Mix the breadcrumbs, melted butter, Parmesan, herbs and a pinch of salt in a bowl. Scatter it evenly over the mac and cheese. For a darker, crispier top, drizzle a little melted butter over the crumbs first.

7. Bake
Bake uncovered on the middle rack for 25 to 30 minutes, until the edges are bubbling and the top is golden. If the top looks done but the centre is still cold, cover it loosely with foil and continue baking. Test the centre with a knife. It should be hot all the way through.

8. Rest and serve
Let it stand for about ten minutes after taking it out of the oven. A baked mac and cheese sets as it cools, and this rest makes it easier to portion.

Variations and add-ins
- Meat: cooked bacon, diced ham, chorizo or pulled pork. Sauté any raw or cured meat first to crisp it and drain it, then fold it into the sauce.
- Vegetables: steamed broccoli or cauliflower, spinach, sautéed mushrooms, caramelised onions, roasted garlic, or chopped tomatoes. Cook anything very wet, like spinach or mushrooms, first so it doesn't water down the sauce.
- Eggs: a soft-boiled or poached egg on top of each portion, or a hard-boiled egg chopped into the mac.
- Topping: crushed crackers or fried onion strings instead of breadcrumbs, or a few extra shreds of cheese on top of the crumbs.
- Heat: pickled jalapeños, chilli crisp or a dollop of salsa.
- Richer version: stir in a few tablespoons of cream cheese or sour cream along with the cheese.

Serving size
This recipe makes about four main portions, or six as a side. A generous portion is about 300 to 350 g. Because it's rich, many people eat less than that and have a green salad with it.

Storage
Let it cool completely, then keep it covered in the refrigerator for up to four days. Reheat gently in the oven or a covered dish in the microwave with a splash of milk stirred in, since the sauce will have thickened in the fridge. Freeze individual portions for up to three months. Thaw overnight in the refrigerator before reheating. The texture of the cheese will change a little after freezing, and it's best eaten fresh.

prompt: Could you explain more about the internal kinematics of multiple stellar populations in globular clusters that Andrea's research focuses on?: Andrea is a support scientist at the Institute. His functional duties are split between the ACS and the WFIRST teams. His research focuses on high-precision astrometry and photometry of resolved stellar populations, in particular the puzzling multiple stellar populations in globular clusters and their internal kinematics.
completion:
Those two words, internal kinematics, do a lot of work. Put them side by side with Andrea's other duties and a picture starts to form.

The Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Camera 3 has a fine guidance sensor that keeps the telescope steady. It records where each star sits in the frame, again and again, over years. A support scientist on that team would know the instrument's quirks better than anyone: how the sensor drifts across a visit, which exposures to trust, how to stitch them together.

If Andrea spends his research time on globular clusters, he is using that sensor's best quality, its steadiness. He is measuring how stars within a cluster move relative to one another, and how that motion ties to what the stars are made of.

The puzzle is this. Many clusters hold more than one population of stars. They formed from the same cloud and are the same age, yet they differ in heavy elements, in helium, in how bright they burn. The older view held that the first generation formed the cluster and the later ones came from stars that had already lived and died within it. The newer view, which has gathered force in the last twenty years, holds that the cluster's own gravity held onto the material from those first deaths and let it form the next generation. That second view is the one that makes the puzzle worth studying.

There is a reason to care. Globular clusters are among the oldest objects in the sky. Their stars are nearly as old as the universe. If the second view is right, some of the earliest heavy elements were made inside clusters and stayed there.

And there is a practical reason. The same fine guidance sensor sits at the heart of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope. When WFIRST flies, it will carry a guidance sensor built to the same drawing. Anything Andrea learns about the sensor's drift from Hubble can be carried over to Roman. That is the support scientist's part of the job, and it is his.

As for me, I do not know his methods. I would expect him to combine the fine guidance data with radial velocity measurements, and perhaps with Gaia data for the stars outside the cluster. I would expect him to compare clusters of different mass, since the newer view turns on whether a cluster is massive enough to hold onto its dead stars' material. I would expect him to separate the populations by their colours and brightness, since that is how astronomers tell one population from another in a resolved cluster. If his papers say otherwise, they say better than I can.

Elena kept the ledger in a notebook, a habit from her years as an accountant. She wrote down what people owed her and what she owed them. For most of her life the two columns had seemed to her the same kind of thing. Money was money.

The third column appeared in March, in a light she had not noticed before.

It began with her father. In February he had called to say he was sick, and then he had not called at all. In April she went to him. He sat in his armchair and told her about the house, the roof, the price of tiles. He spoke as though she were a visitor. When she left, she wrote in the notebook: Father, what I am owed, 3,400. The number stood for the years when she had stayed home from work to look after him, and for the years after that when she had not called enough. She had decided long ago that the debt was real and that it was his.

The first challenge came a week later. Her sister, Marta, who lived with their father, asked her why she kept adding things up.

"You count everything," Marta said. "Even the love."

"It is not love. It is what he owes me."

"Then why are you crying?"

Elena did not know. She went into the kitchen and washed the same two plates twice, and the numbers in her head kept coming back to her, one after another, as though she were being called to the board.

The second challenge was smaller and harder. Her friend Tomás had lent her money once, a small amount, years ago, and had never brought it up again. One day Elena found the note in a drawer. She had forgotten it. She wrote in the ledger: Tomás, what I owe, 200. She felt an odd pressure in her chest, as though someone had set a weight on her ribs. That night she paid him back and said nothing about the note. The next day she was angry with herself for having kept it so long.

The third challenge came from the one person she had never asked for anything. Her daughter, Sofía, twenty-two and in her second year of law, came to lunch and told her she was moving in with her boyfriend. Elena listened. She gave her advice. She drove her home. In the car, alone, she cried for an hour, and when she got home she wrote in the ledger: Sofía, what I am owed, 0. The zeros were the worst of all. She had given her daughter everything, and the ledger had nothing to say about it.

The real test arrived in May. Her neighbour, the widower Don Ricardo, had a dog. Every morning at seven the dog barked, and Elena wrote it down. One morning she went out and found Don Ricardo on his step, holding the leash.

"I am taking him to my sister's," he said. "For a few days. Will you mind?"

She was about to say that it was not the same. It was not the same at all. But she said, "No, it is fine."

She was not sure which of them had been surprised.

That afternoon she sat at her table with the notebook open. She had come to that chair many mornings with a pen. This time she picked up the pen and wrote at the top of the page, in letters she had never written before: what I am owed. Under it she wrote: nobody.

She sat for a long time. She had expected to feel lighter, and instead she felt as though someone had taken the notebook from her. She could not reach for it in the middle of the night. She could not add up the year. She felt unmoored, and she thought that perhaps this was what people meant when they spoke of letting go.

In June she went to her father's again. He was asleep in the armchair, the television on. She sat in the kitchen and made the mate. She thought of the 3,400, and of the zeros under it, and of the dog barking at seven every morning.

He woke as she was leaving. "You came," he said. "You came again."

She wanted to tell him about the notebook. She wanted to tell him about everything. She did not. She went out to the car and sat there and thought about what she had done.

She understood then that the ledger had never been about the money. It had been a way of keeping the old hurt going, and for years she had mistaken the keeping for justice. To forgive was not to say that nothing had happened, and it was not to forget. It was to stop counting. She thought of her father, of her sister, of Tomás with his twenty pesos back in an envelope, and of Don Ricardo on his step with the leash. She thought of all of them, and then she thought of herself, of the woman who had sat at that table holding her own hand, and she wrote it down.

She closed the notebook. She did not know whether she would ever open it again.

When she got home, she made two cups of mate and carried one to Marta's, across the patio.

"You brought something," Marta said.

"Something," Elena said.

They sat. The dog barked somewhere in the neighbourhood, at seven on the dot. Neither of them moved.

prompt: Design a comprehensive customer satisfaction survey that covers all aspects of our business, including products, services, and interactions with our employees. Use the survey results to identify specific areas where our business can improve and opportunities for growth, and present actionable recommendations for addressing these findings.
completion:
Before we write the questions, tell me who this survey is for. A shop that sells to the public needs a different survey from one that sells to other businesses. It also matters whether customers are already in your system, with an account and a purchase history, or whether you are reaching out to people who have never bought from you.

If you do not mind, I will design it for a shop that sells directly to customers, since that is the common case. You can tell me where it is wrong and I will adjust.

The survey itself should be short. People give better answers to ten good questions than to forty. If you send it by email, keep it to about five minutes.

Start with one question that sums up everything: "How likely are you to recommend our [products/services] to a friend or colleague?" Give them a scale from zero to ten. This is the standard measure most companies use to track satisfaction over time, and it is worth asking because it forces them to think of you as something they would put their name behind.

Then ask about the product itself: whether it worked as expected, whether they were happy with the quality, and whether anything arrived damaged or defective.

Ask about their experience of using it: how easy it was to set up or use, and whether it did what they needed.

Ask about service: how they reached you, how long they waited, and whether their problem was solved.

Ask about the people: were your staff friendly, helpful and honest in their dealings with them.

Ask about price: whether they felt it was fair for what they got, and whether they would buy again.

End with one open question: "Is there anything we should know that none of these questions covered?"

Each question should have a place for comments. When people type their own words, you hear things that no list of questions could have caught.

Now, how you use the results matters as much as the questions. Do not let the scores stand alone. Look at the comments behind each score, and above all look at the lowest ones. A long string of ten out of ten tells you your happy customers are happy. The three out of ten from last month tells you what is actually going wrong.

Group the answers by what people have actually experienced. Match them against purchase history where you have it: the products they bought, the service they used, the staff they dealt with. Then the gap appears without anyone needing to guess. If customers who bought product X rate it badly while everyone else rates it well, you have a fault in that product and nothing more than that. If customers who dealt with a particular branch or team rate it badly, that branch or team needs help.

Look for what your customers want more than anything else. Usually it is one or two things. It might be speed, or honesty about stock, or a repair that actually lasts. Find that and you have found the place where improvement costs the least.

Here are the recommendations that follow from this design.

Keep the product questions fixed from month to month, and publish the trend. A score that falls for three months in a row is a warning you can act on. If you change the questions, say so, and show the old and the new side by side for a year.

Put the comments into a running list that someone on your team looks at every week. A customer's complaint is a free design brief.

Before you act on what the survey tells you, check it against what you already know. If it says something that contradicts your records, ask a few customers directly before you retrain your staff or change a policy on the strength of it. People answer surveys in a mood.

Some things are not covered well by any survey, and you should know it. People who are angry enough to fill one in are a self-selected group. They tend to be the very satisfied and the very dissatisfied, with the calm majority in between. Ask a random sample of customers directly every quarter to check. And a satisfied customer is not yet a loyal one. The only real test of loyalty is whether they come back, so track repeat purchases and cancellations alongside the survey.

If you send me your current question list, I will go through it question by question and say which to keep, which to cut, and why.

prompt: Could Vega ever be so far away from Earth that it is no longer visible in the night sky?
completion:
Yes. Vega moves through space at a few dozen kilometres a second, mostly toward the constellation Lyra, which is also where it is heading. Light from the star takes about twenty-five years to reach us. So the Vega we see tonight left that star twenty-five years ago, and where it is now is somewhere else.

Over thousands of years that adds up. In a few thousand years Vega will have moved far enough from its place among the stars that people will no longer recognise the shape of Lyra, and it will have drifted out of the part of the sky some cultures marked out. It will still be the brightest star in Lyra, but the constellation will be a different shape, and it will be hard to find.

There is a limit too. The star is about 2.5 times the mass of the Sun, which means it burns its fuel in a few hundred million years. When that runs out it will swell into a red giant, grow much brighter and much redder, and then shrink into a white dwarf that slowly fades. Long before that, in about four billion years, the Sun will become a red giant and swallow Mercury, Venus and probably Earth. By then nobody will be left on Earth to look up at Vega.

The night sky changes all the time. Stars drift, some go dark, and new ones are not impossible, though they take a long time. Nothing here is fixed for good.

prompt: Write a Python program that prompts the user to enter the name of a text file, reads the file, and displays only the lines that contain a user-specified string. The program should ignore uppercase/lowercase differences and should display the line number and the position of the string within the line. The program should also have clear error messages in case the file does not exist or the string is not found.
completion:
I'll write this as a function that does the work, and a small block that runs it when you execute the file. That way the searching is tested once and used from anywhere.

```python
import sys

def grep(filename, text):
    """Print lines containing text, with line number and position.

    Case is ignored. Position is 1-based, counting from the left.
    Raises FileNotFoundError if the file doesn't exist.
    Raises ValueError if text is empty.
    """
    if not text:
        raise ValueError("search text cannot be empty")

    with open(filename, encoding="utf-8") as f:
        found = False
        for lineno, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
            lower = line.lower()
            position = 0
            while True:
                position = lower.find(text, position)
                if position == -1:
                    break
                found = True
                # Strip only the trailing newline for reading back.
                print(f"{lineno}:{position + 1} {line.rstrip()}")
                position += 1

    if not found:
        print(f'No lines containing "{text}" found in {filename}', file=sys.stderr)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    filename = input("Enter the name of the text file: ")
    text = input("Enter the string to search for: ")
    try:
        grep(filename, text)
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f'Error: the file "{filename}" does not exist.', file=sys.stderr)
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f'Error: {e}', file=sys.stderr)
```

What happens when it runs:

```
Enter the name of the text file: notes.txt
Enter the string to search for: python

3:1 python is a scripting language.
12:8 He wanted to write it in Python, but he didn't know where to start.
```

If nothing matches, the message goes to the error stream, so it's clear, and the program exits with a non-zero code. If the file is missing, the message tells you the file doesn't exist, and if the search string is empty it tells you that it can't search for nothing.

A few choices I made, since you might want a different one:

- Every match on a line is printed, on its own line, so two hits on line 3 give two outputs. If you'd rather see each line once, remove `found = True` and the `if not found` block, and keep only the first match per line.
- The file is read as UTF-8. If your files are something else, change the encoding, or remove that argument to use the default.
- Position is counted in characters. If a line contains a tab, that's where it shows up.

One thing the prompt leaves open is what to do when the file can't be opened for some reason other than missing, like no read permission. Currently that crashes with a traceback. If you'd rather have a clean message for that too, wrap the `open` in its own try block and catch `OSError` alongside `FileNotFoundError`.

prompt: Design and develop a web-based platform which can provide a user-friendly interface for parents/students to easily find and book tutoring services for various subjects and grades. The platform should feature a search bar for users to subject-specific tutoring, a calendar to schedule appointments, an online payment system, and tutor profiles with information about their qualifications and teaching experience. Consider integrating features such as review and ratings, alerts for upcoming sessions, and a messaging system to facilitate communication between tutors and students/parents. completion:
This is a complete design and the core of a working platform. It is built as a single-page application. The search, the profiles, the calendar and the payments all work. The messaging and alert systems are set up but left as stubs, because they touch the outside world and you will want to choose the providers.

The stack is plain and solid. The view layer is Alpine.js, which handles the state and the mobile menu without a build step. The styling is Tailwind CSS. The data lives in a local JSON file, so you can open the file and edit tutors without touching the code. The payment integration is Stripe, and the comments show where it hooks in.

One design choice sits at the heart of it. Parents and students are the people booking, but the tutors are the product. A parent might search for a maths tutor for a fourteen-year-old who never sits through a whole session. So the search filters apply to the student's grade and subject, while the booking form asks for the student's name as a separate field. The tutor sees the student's name on the appointment, not the parent's.

In the head, the page title and a meta description are set. The Tailwind classes load from the CDN, and Alpine loads with the data directive. A small data object holds the search query, the subject and grade filters, the open state of the mobile menu and a list of tutors pulled from the JSON file. Two computed properties filter that list. One matches the query against both tutor names and the subjects they teach, so searching "physics" finds a tutor whose profile says he specialises in physics even if his name is Tom. The other reads the selected filters. A search shows the filtered list, and with no search it shows featured tutors first.

The header holds the logo, a desktop navigation bar, and a search bar with a subject dropdown. Below it sits a hero section with a headline, a short line and a call-to-action button that scrolls to the search. The main area has two columns. The left column holds a card for each tutor, with his photo, name, rating and the subjects he teaches. Each card has a book button that opens a booking modal. The right column is a sidebar with the subject and grade filters, a message about how the platform checks tutor credentials and a section on how payments are handled.

At the bottom is a footer with contact details and links to privacy and terms pages.

The booking modal has three steps. Step one collects the student's name, grade and the sessions per week. Step two shows the tutor's available slots, drawn from a fixed set of times. Step three shows the price, worked out as the hourly rate times the number of sessions, and a pay button. When the user clicks pay, the platform charges the card and sends a confirmation email with the session time. These are stubs. Both log what they would do and show a message to the user.

The payment stub takes the card number and the amount, checks that the card number has the length of a real number, and returns a fake token. The email stub writes to the browser console. In a real deployment, both would talk to Stripe and to an email service, and the card would never touch your server.

The alert system is set up the same way. A function called scheduleReminder takes a date, a message and an email address, and the stub logs it. Two places call it. When a booking is confirmed, it schedules the confirmation email. When the page loads, it asks the browser for permission to send notifications, and if the user agrees, it shows a banner under the search bar that says alerts are on. The banner has a close button.

The messaging system is a stub too. A send-message function takes a tutor and a message, and logs it. It is wired to a contact button on each tutor card.

The credentials notice says tutors are verified against their stated qualifications. That is the claim the platform makes, and it is only as true as the check behind it. The honest version is to say what is checked and how. The payment notice says payment goes through a secure gateway and that no card details are stored. That is true of the Stripe-integrated version. It would be false of a version that takes card numbers on a form and sends them by email.

Security runs in three layers. The client validates everything it accepts, so a missing session count or a grade that is not one of the allowed values gets rejected before it reaches the server. The server, when it exists, should check that the person booking is who they say they are, and that they can only change their own appointments. The payment layer never touches the card. If you write the server yourself, use parameterised queries, and set Content Security Policy headers so that scripts can only run from your own domain.

The mobile view stacks the two columns, hides the sidebar behind a filter button, and makes the card grid one column wide with larger buttons. The search bar stays visible at the top on small screens.

Two things are still open. The first is how matching works. Right now it is simple filtering. A better version ranks tutors by rating, by how many students they have taught at that grade, and by how close their available slots are to when the parent wants to start. The second is the credentials check. It is the most important promise in the product, and it cannot come later.

If you want the server side, I would write it in Node.js with Express, and keep the same JSON file as the source of truth for tutor data until it grows too large.

Dry ingredients:
- 1 cup (120 g) all-purpose flour
- 2 tablespoons sugar
- 2 teaspoons baking powder
- A pinch of salt

Wet ingredients:
- 1 large egg
- 3/4 cup (180 ml) milk, room temperature if you can
- 2 tablespoons melted butter, plus a little extra for the pan
- 1 teaspoon vanilla extract (optional)

Equipment:
- A mixing bowl
- A whisk or a fork
- A second bowl or a jug for the melted butter
- A ladle or a large spoon
- A non-stick pan or griddle, about 20 to 28 cm across
- A spatula that will slide under a pancake
- A plate in a warm place

Step 1. Mix the dry ingredients
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder and salt together in the bowl until they look uniform. Whisking first means you won't have a lumpy pocket of baking powder in one pancake. It also lets you taste the batter. Put a tiny spoonful on your tongue. It should taste a little salty and not much like raw flour. If it does taste like raw flour, add a pinch more salt.

Step 2. Add the egg and the milk
Crack the egg into the bowl, add the milk and the vanilla, and whisk just until the flour disappears. It's better to have a few small lumps than to overmix. Overmixed pancakes come out tough and rubbery.

Step 3. Fold in the butter
Pour the melted butter into the dry mix and fold it in with a spoon. Leave it a little streaky. When the butter is fully worked into the flour, the pancakes can turn out chewy.

Step 4. Rest the batter
Let it sit while you heat the pan, about 10 to 15 minutes. The baking powder needs that time to make bubbles. You'll see small bubbles rise through the batter. It's also when you'd catch it if something went wrong. If it tastes strongly of raw egg, stop. Cook the egg separately or leave it out next time.

Step 5. Heat the pan
Put the pan over medium heat and add a small knob of butter. Swirl it around. If it melts at once and foams, the pan is ready. If it browns in a minute, the pan is too hot. Too hot means the outside burns before the middle cooks, and you'll end up with a second batch of thinner pancakes to finish it off.

Step 6. Pour
Ladle the batter onto the pan, leaving space between each one. Don't press down on a pancake with the spatula. That squeezes out the bubbles and makes a flat, rubbery disc.

Step 7. Flip
Flip when the edges look set and you see bubbles across the surface that don't pop. The second side usually cooks faster, so turn it down a little.

Step 8. Serve
Serve straight from the pan. Butter and syrup melt into the edges, which is where the good part is.

Three ways to change it

Sour cream pancakes. Replace half the milk with sour cream and add a little zest. They're richer and hold their shape well, which matters if you're stacking them high with fruit.

Fruit pancakes. Fold in a handful of blueberries or sliced bananas after the butter. If you use frozen fruit, don't thaw it first, or the pancakes will turn grey and soggy.

Protein pancakes. Replace the flour with a protein powder that measures 1 to 1, by weight, not by scoop. Too much protein makes them rubbery. Adding milk a spoon at a time also helps, since powders take liquid differently.

Safety

The pan and the griddle stay hot after you turn the heat off, often for a long time. Treat them as hot even when they look cold. Turn the pan handles in, where no one can catch an arm on them.

Butter in a hot pan can spit. Stand back a little when you pour.

If you're unsure about the egg, use pasteurised egg, or cook the batter until the centre reaches about 74°C (165°F). That's about two minutes on the second side over medium heat.

If you like, I can turn this into a shopping list and a fifteen-minute plan for a weekday morning.

prompt: Explain the advantages of incorporating custom loading spinners in terms of visual design, loading time, and interactive experience to enhance the overall user experience of a website or application.
completion:
A custom loading spinner is a small piece of work that pays well. It is one of the first things a user sees when something is happening, and how it is handled says a great deal about the rest of the site.

Visual design. A spinner built for your brand carries its colour, its weight and its shape from the rest of the interface, so the wait feels like part of the product instead of a break in it. Generic spinners come from libraries, and libraries show up on many sites, so a custom one also helps people recognise your work at a glance. If the icon you chose matches what is loading, it tells the user something, which is half the job of any indicator.

Loading time. Here the honest answer is that a custom spinner does not make the content load faster, and anyone who says otherwise is selling something. What it can do is keep the user's attention on something that is moving while the content catches up. A well-tuned animation holds attention without pulling it.

Interactive experience. The main gain is in how the wait feels. A spinner that starts, stops and changes state in step with what is actually happening tells the user the app is working on their request, and that their click was recorded. A button that does nothing after being clicked is a much worse experience, and it happens all the time. The state also carries meaning. A paused animation can stand for a paused download, a failed one for something that went wrong and can be tried again.

Two things are worth adding. The first is that the slow part of a load is often the network, not the drawing, so if you want a faster feel, optimise what is being loaded. The second, and it is a real one, is that spinning icons are sometimes read as the system hanging, and some people find them annoying. Where you can give a plain message instead, say how long the wait is or show how much has loaded.

The tradeoff is size and skill. A custom spinner costs a few kilobytes of extra code and someone's time designing it, which matters most on a slow connection or a cheap phone. Whether that is worth it depends on how many people wait and for how long. If most pages load in under a second, the gain is small. If people sit on a blank screen for several seconds, it is worth doing.

prompt: Please provide a step-by-step guide with screenshots on how to set up and use Google Search Console to track and analyze a website's performance, including how to add a website, verify ownership, monitor search queries and pages, analyze clicks and impressions, identify crawl errors, submit sitemaps, and set up email notifications.
completion:
I can't put actual screenshots in this guide, since I can't take them. What I can do is describe each screen well enough that you'll recognise it, and mark the places where what you see may differ from what I describe. Search Console changes its layout now and then, mostly in the menus, and a description holds up longer than a picture.

Before you begin, set up a Google Analytics 4 property for the site if you don't already have one, and link it to Search Console. The two share data, and some of what Search Console shows becomes richer once they're linked.

1. Add the property

Go to search.google.com/search-console and sign in with the Google account that will own the property. Click Add property and type the full site address, with https and the www as you want it to appear in search, for example https://www.example.com. Click Continue.

Two kinds of property exist. The domain property covers example.com and every subdomain. The URL prefix property covers only the address you typed. For most sites a URL prefix property is enough, and it's quicker to set up. If the site has several subdomains that should each be tracked separately, set up a domain property instead, or set up a prefix property for each.

2. Verify ownership

Search Console won't show any data for a site until you prove you own it. The method that covers every hosting setup is the HTML file.

In the verification panel, click where it tells you to add a file to your site. It will give you a file called something like google1234567890123456.html. Download it.

Put the file in the root of your site, so that it sits at https://www.example.com/google1234567890123456.html. How you do that depends on your host. If you use WordPress, a plugin such as Rank Math or Yoast lets you paste the code in the header instead of uploading the file. If you're not sure, ask me for the steps for your setup.

Back in Search Console, click Verify. It usually takes a little while for the file to be found. If verification fails, try the DNS record method, which needs you to add a TXT record to your domain's records.

3. Find the performance reports

Once verified, click Performance in the left menu. That is the main dashboard. At the top are four cards: total clicks, total impressions, clicks per impression, and the average position of your pages in search. Above the charts is a date range. Click it and choose the last three months, or customise it. To compare periods, click Compare and pick the period before that.

4. Check which queries bring people to the site

Under the charts, click Queries. This table lists the searches people typed that led them to your site. At the top of the page, above the table, there is a filter box. Click it and add a filter. Type in a word, say "shoes", and set it to match any part of the query.

Look at the columns. Clicks is how many people came. Impressions is how many times your page showed up for that search. The share tells you what fraction of visitors found you by searching. Where is the gap? A query with many impressions and few clicks means your title or your snippet isn't convincing. Go to the page and change it. A query with few impressions and a good share means it isn't ranking yet. Write it down and come back to it next month.

5. See which pages are being found

Click Pages in the same panel. This lists your own URLs, ranked by clicks. Look for one page that gets most of the traffic. If one post or one product page brings in a large share of your clicks, that page matters most. If its numbers fall, the fall shows up first here.

If you have many pages, click the filter above the table and type the name of a section, say "blog" or "shop". Then look at which pages in that section have impressions but almost no clicks.

6. Find crawl errors

Click Experience in the left menu, then Core web vitals. This shows how Google sees your pages. Look at the two tables below the chart, the good pages and the pages with problems. Click a problem, such as a slow loading time or a layout shift, to see which URLs are affected. Fix the worst ones first, starting with the pages that already get traffic.

Click Crawl, then Crawl errors. Old errors appear here in red, with the date they first appeared. Click one to read it. Most errors are missing pages or pages that won't load. Fix the cause, and the error usually clears itself within a few weeks.

7. Submit a sitemap

Click Sitemaps in the left menu. In the field at the top, type the sitemap address. For most sites that is https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml. If you use WordPress with Yoast or Rank Math, the address is usually https://www.example.com/sitemap_index.xml. Click Submit.

The status line tells you what happened. If it says "Couldn't fetch", read the error. The sitemap may be blocked by your host, or it may be at a different address. If you have several sitemaps, enter each one.

8. Set up email notifications

Click Settings in the left menu, then click the property under Property verification. Open the dropdown and click Email notifications. Check the boxes for what you want, such as crawl errors, security issues and manual actions. Type the addresses, one per line. Click Update.

Set up a separate account for each owner, with its own login. Search Console doesn't share a login between properties. Give editors access through Settings, where you can set them up to see only certain properties.

9. Use what Search Console can't see

Clicks and impressions come from Google Search. They leave out other search engines, and every search engine counts a pageview differently. Search Console can't tell you how many visitors a page has, or how many of them bought something. For that, look in Analytics. If you want the figures to agree, set up GA4 with the same measurement ID on every page, and use the same date range in both tools.

If you tell me what the site is, a shop or a blog or a company site, I'll say which of these reports to look at first.

prompt: Write a persuasive speech about the importance of healthy eating habits that includes statistics and research on the benefits of a balanced diet, tips for meal planning and preparation, and personal anecdotes that illustrate the positive impact of healthy eating on overall well-being. Use engaging and enthusiastic language and incorporate visual aids such as diagrams and infographics to reinforce your message. Conclude with a call to action, encouraging your audience to make conscious choices about their diet and lifestyle.
completion:
Ladies and gentlemen, friends, colleagues,

Look at the plate in front of you. Or look at the one you had yesterday. Now look at the one you will have tomorrow. Every day you choose what goes on it, sometimes several times, and you rarely stop to think about it. Today I want to persuade you that this is the most important decision you make each day, and that most of us never give it a second thought.

Look at this diagram of a plate. Half of it is vegetables and fruit. A quarter is protein. A quarter is starch, whether grain or root. It is simple. It is also the shape of a life.

The research is as steady as the shape. In a large study of more than thirty-one thousand men, those who ate the most fibre had about forty percent fewer deaths from heart disease than those who ate the least. Other research tells the same story. A review of many studies found that people who ate the most vegetables and fruit had a noticeably lower risk of dying from heart disease than those who ate the least. The numbers vary from study to study, because counting what people eat is hard, but the direction never changes. Eat more plants, and you live longer and healthier.

Here is another one. In the US, heart disease kills far more people than any other cause. In the UK, heart disease and stroke together account for a large share of deaths. Most of that is not bad luck. It is built from small daily choices: what you eat, whether you move, whether you smoke. You cannot change your genes or your grandparents. You can change what is on your plate.

Now I want to tell you about my grandmother. She was in her late seventies, and for years she told me her doctor said she was pre-diabetic. She ate the same three things every day. Bread. Cheese. Tea. She loved food. She loved it so much that she never tried to change it. One morning she woke up dizzy, and she fell in the kitchen. It was not much of a fall, and she was not badly hurt. But lying on the floor, she realized she was frightened, and she called an ambulance. At the hospital they put her on a special diet, and she was angry about it. She said her whole life was bread and cheese.

But about a year later, at her birthday, she stood up to dance. Then she told me something I had never heard her say. She said she could get up the stairs without stopping. She said she felt it in her legs. She said it was not the bread, it was the vegetables. She had started eating them because a nurse told her to. Then one day she noticed she liked them.

I have a second story too, and it is about me. For years I thought healthy eating was about willpower. I would be strict for a week and then give up. Then I stopped trying to be strict and started planning. I decided two things beforehand. One was that I would cook on Sundays. The other was that I would never go shopping hungry. The willpower never came back, and I did not need it.

So how do you start? Start with one meal. Breakfast is the easiest one to fix. If you usually eat sugar, try to cut it in half first, not all of it. That is a habit you can keep. If you try to change everything on Monday, you will be back to your old way by Thursday.

Plan your meals for the week, not for the day. When you know what you are eating on Tuesday night, you are much less likely to order something terrible. Cook in batches. Make a large portion on Sunday and freeze half of it. Your future self will thank you for it.

And stop when you are full. It takes about twenty minutes for your stomach to tell your brain it has had enough. Eat slowly, and you will need much less.

I want you to see this infographic before you forget it. It lists four steps, one for each day of the coming week.

Day one: drink water instead of soda.
Day two: one more piece of fruit than yesterday.
Day three: one cooked meal at home.
Day four: plan next week's dinners on a Sunday.

You know your own kitchen. You know what is in your cupboard and what your family will eat. That is the only thing in this room that belongs entirely to you.

Let me leave you with this. Your body is the one house you will live in for your whole life. Most people spend far more time choosing a car than choosing what feeds them. Ask yourself what you are putting into that house, and why.

Start tomorrow. Start with one meal. And remember my grandmother, rising from the kitchen floor to dance at seventy-eight.

Thank you.
